prompt:
A crisp studio photograph, taken level with the base, of a classroom demonstration board with three counting trays under the pegs: a flat base with THREE upright pegs marked A (left), B (middle) and C (right), and one shallow empty tray sitting under each peg.

It carries 5 round disks of clearly different widths -- disk 1 (the narrowest) is red, disk 2 is yellow, disk 3 is green, disk 4 is blue, disk 5 is purple (the widest) -- each with its own size number printed large on its face. The stacking rule is the usual one -- a disk rests either on the base or on a disk wider than itself, never on a narrower one.

All 5 disks start stacked on peg A, widest at the bottom, and are moved to peg C in the FEWEST possible moves (exactly 31 moves), one disk at a time, never a wider disk onto a narrower one.

Every time the NARROWEST disk (disk 1) is set down on a peg during that solution, one bead is dropped into the tray under THAT peg. (Its position at the start does not count -- only landings during the solution.) Beads are never taken out again.

Show the finished puzzle -- all 5 disks stacked on peg C -- with the three trays holding the beads they collected: the tray under each peg must contain exactly as many beads as the number of times disk 1 landed on that peg. Draw the beads as separate round beads lying in the tray, countable at a glance.

Keep the picture clean: no move list, no annotations, no captions. The only characters in the image are the letters on the base and the number printed on each disk.
easy_question: Never mind how well it is drawn. Does this picture show a classroom stacking board with three counting trays under the pegs: a base with three upright pegs carrying round stacking disks of graduated widths? A realistic photo, an illustration, a schematic or a clean diagram ALL count as yes. Answer NO only if the image instead shows just a blank card or plain panel that prints an answer with none of that shown, or shows something unrelated. Answer yes or no only.

reference.q_total: Counting the disks on every peg together, how many disks are threaded on the pegs in this picture in total? The board the pegs stand on is NOT a disk. Reply with a single number and nothing else.
reference.q_s_A: Look at the stacking board. Each disk has its size number printed on its face (1 = the narrowest). List the size numbers of the disks on the LEFT peg (A), reading from the bottom disk upward, separated by commas. If a printed number is not legible, use that disk's width rank instead (1 = the narrowest disk in the picture). If that peg carries no disks at all, answer exactly: none . Answer with the list only, no other words.
reference.q_c_A: Look at the stacking board. Count the disks threaded on the LEFT peg (A): HOW MANY disks does that one peg carry right now? Do NOT answer with the number printed on a disk, and do not count the board the pegs stand on -- answer how many disks are stacked on that peg (0 if it is empty). Reply with a single digit and nothing else.
